en: The Commentary on the Śrīmaitrāyaṇīya-Mānava-Gṛhyasūtra. First Chapter.
First Section.
Now begins the Mānava Gṛhyasūtra.
Oṃ. From the initiation ceremony onwards, he shall be one who observes the vows. (ManGS 1.1.1)

Wearing garments of bark, with matted hair, subsisting on alms, carrying a staff of *śalka* wood, he shall wear a girdle of *muñja* grass; he shall not be contrary to his teacher and shall perform all tasks for him. (Manava-Gṛhya-Sūtra 1.1.2)
Whatever he might approach, that he should give to him; among many, that with which he is connected.
One should not enter his bedchamber.
He should not wear [garments] that have fringes.
He shall not mount a chariot.
One should not speak untruth.
One should not look at a woman who has been robbed.
One should not speak for the sake of dwelling.
One should not hold onto anything for the sake of pleasure.
One should avoid all things that come into contact with women.
He should not consume honey, meat, alkaline substances, or salt.
He shall not bathe, nor shall he step into water.
If he should bathe, he would float in the water like a staff.
Having gone out before sunset, he should bring two pieces of firewood; "for one desiring spiritual luster," so says the Śruti. (ManGS 1.1.15)

Having swept around the fire with the words, "This hymn for the worthy one," having sprinkled water around it, and having strewn grass around it, he places a fuel-stick on the fire with the words, "May we prosper through this fuel";
he places a second stick with the words, "Thou art fuel; may we prosper. (Manava Gṛhya Sūtra 1.1.16)
With the words, "Today I have entered the waters," he worships [the water].
"When you first undertook austerity as austerity and entered upon the life of a student, may we be dear to sacred learning, long-lived, and wise"—with these words he wipes his face. (ManGS 1.1.18)
"May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods," with these words he touches his two ears.
"May we see what is auspicious with our eyes, O worshipful ones"—with these words [he touches] the two eyes.
"May we, praising with firm colors and our bodies, attain that life ordained by the gods"—with these words he touches the limbs.
"Here is steadfastness, here is self-steadfastness"—with these words, he mutters [the mantra] beginning from the region of the heart.
"Bestow radiance upon us," with these words he takes hold of the earth.
"The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Agastya;
that which is the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine. Having thus touched his limbs with ashes, he purifies himself with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses.
Thus ends the first section. //1//
The second section.
Om. Now, he performs the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).

Before sunset, having gone out to the north or east of the village and sat down in a clean place, having sipped water and filled his joined palms with water, he turns to the right and invokes [the Gāyatrī] with the verse: "Come hither, O Virāj, O Goddess, the imperishable one, equal to Brahman; O Mother of the meters, Gāyatrī, favor this prayer of mine. (ManGS 1.2.2)

Having recited "The first vigor you are," and having joined [the horse] with "Who joins you?", he yokes it eight times with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyam. Thus the desires are prescribed.
Then [he recites] the Triṣṭubh verse beginning with "The god goes forth" for the one who desires kingship, and the Jagatī verse beginning with "They yoke" for the Vaiśya. ManGS 1.2.3.
Having recited the two verses beginning with "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam," he releases [the horse] with the words "Who releases you? and pours out a handful of water.
In this same manner, he stands at dawn.

By this rule, whatever Brāhmaṇa, Rājanya, or Vaiśya practices the life of a student for twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, or forty-eight years—whether shaven-headed, with a topknot and matted hair, or entirely matted-haired; whether covered in dirt, weak, or emaciated—he, having bathed, obtains everything that he desires in his mind. // ManGS 1.2.6 //
By this rite, he has studied well.
Having understood the meanings of the Vedic hymns, one who intends to perform the sacrifice should have a cow brought.
A learned Vedic scholar should honor his teacher.
If he is merely a reciter of the Vedas and not a knower of their meaning, for him there is no ceremonial bath.
Having bathed with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and with the two verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ," he puts on two unwashed garments.
"You are wealth; make me wealthy. For the sake of splendor, for brilliance, and for the luster of sacred knowledge, I entrust you to [him]," with these words he entrusts him. (ManGS 1.2.12)
"Just as heaven and earth neither fear nor suffer harm,
so may my breath not suffer harm," with these words he anoints himself.
He ties on a piece of gold.
He holds the parasol, the staff, the garland, and the perfume. ManGS_1,2.15 //
"O two deities, Heaven and Earth, you who are the foundation, stand firm; do not cause me to suffer," [with these words] he puts on his sandals.
From that time forward he wears two garments; therefore, beautiful clothing should be worn—so says the Śruti.
Having taken leave of his teachers and his kinsmen, he should go to his own home.
It is forbidden for her to exit through a back door, to dress together with a woman in soiled clothes,
to sleep on the same bed as a menstruating woman, to speak harsh words to her teacher, and to lie down, smile, run, stand, walk, sing, or look at him in an improper place.
On the full moon day or on the new moon day, he should sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Agni.
Having eaten the *pavi* as he pleases, from that point onward he may consume honey, meat, alkaline substances, and salt.
Thus ends the second section.
The Third Section.
If the sun should rise or set upon one who knows this, he should, having awakened, recite:
"May my sensory power return to me; may my life return to me; may my fortune return to me."
"May wealth come back to me; may Brahmanhood come back to me.
And may these fires, established on their hearths, arrange themselves here according to their proper places"—thus he recites when the sun has risen.

"May my self return, may my life-span return, may my breath return, may my intention return. May Vaiśvānara, increasing by his choice, stand within me—the mind, the banner of immortality. With these words, he recites [the mantra] after sunset. Or both [husband and wife] should recite it when the sun has risen; or both should recite it after sunset.

If he should perform forbidden acts, or revile [others], or eat the food of one whose food should not be eaten, or if his right eye should twitch, or his ear should ring, or if he should climb onto a fire-altar,
or go to a cemetery, or touch a corpse, or if his semen should be emitted— he should offer an oblation with these two very mantras;
or he may place two fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter into the fire, or he may simply mutter the two mantras.
In this way, one should practice the gross form of unrighteousness. *Manava-Grihya-Sutra* 1.3.5.

In the coarse [forest], he should live by gleaning; unclothed, covered only by hair and skin, he should enter the fire, or die in battle, or even while kindling the fire, he should devote himself to austerity.
Thus ends the third section.
The fourth section:
During the rainy season, one begins the private recitation of the Veda under the asterism Śravaṇā.
He offers the oblation:
"Thou art the nameless one; let thy brilliance go to the camel. For I have indeed received the wisdom of the Father from the nectar; I am born like the sun, svāhā!"
You are named Sarasvatī; you are named Sarasvant. You are named Yukti; you are named Yojas. You are named Mati; you are named Manā.
"May I attain her splendor through the female camel;
may we attain his splendor through the male camel"—this [formula] is appended everywhere. (ManGS 1.4.2)
"Yuje svāhā! Prayuje svāhā! Udyuje svāhā!"—with these [mantras], one who desires the application (yoga) of his students [should sacrifice]. (ManGS 1.4.3)
Then, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he mutters:
"I shall speak the *ṛta*; I shall speak the truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker.
May my speech be established in my mind."
"May my mind be established in speech; bestow long life upon me. You are the voices of the Veda. Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, that [splendor] of Savitṛ. (ManGS 1.4.4)
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he recites the *Sāvitrī* three times, then thirty initial sections (*anuvāka*), and [the section] beginning with "Who indeed yokes? (*ko vā yunakti*).
And [he recites]: "We commence the study; may the Vedic meters attend us. (ManGS 1.4.5)

Its days of non-study are: when the wind blows up a mass [of dust]; from the time rain begins with the appearance of flakes or spray until it stops; when lightning flashes but does not thunder—according to the Śruti, such a storm caused by the gods lasts for the duration of the event; when there is thunder accompanied by lightning, clouds, and meteors, or when there are indistinct sounds [of thunder]; and other occasions according to traditional practice.
Having studied for four and a half months, or five and a half months, he performs the ritual of dismissal.
Then he mutters: "I have spoken the Truth; may it protect me, may it protect the speaker; may it protect me, may it protect the speaker.
Vāk is established in my mind; my mind is established in Vāk. Bestow long life upon me.
You are the voices of the Veda."
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; that [splendor] of Savitṛ... (ManGS 1.4.8).

Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he recites the *Sāvitrī* three times; and he recites the first three sections of the *Amu* [the *Vimocana* section], saying: "Who unbinds you? Having unbound [the fire], he says: "We release the fires from their vows; let the *Chandas* breathe again. (ManGS 1.4.9)
One should not study on the night of the first day of the lunar fortnight, nor for the duration of two nights thereafter, as long as there are clouds in the sky.
In the case of lightning, thunder, and rain, [the suspension of study] is immediate.

On the days named after the constellations, he should study the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, Kalpas, Medhas, Mahāvratas, Aṣṭāpadīs, and Vaiṣuvatas during the day; on the Vaiṣuvata day itself, he should study with moist hands.
One should not weep at night, nor after eating, nor in a village.
The rule for the *śukriya* [rite] has been explained in the *Pravargya-kalpa*; however, one should close one's eyes during the twenty-third [verse].
One should not utter the names of cows in the presence of cows, nor the words "eight-footed," "semen," or "urine" in the presence of pregnant cows.

One should study during the day the six ṛc-verses dedicated to Āditya and Sūrya, beginning with "O Sūrya, bestow sight upon us" and "Sūrya plunges into the waters," for Śunīśīrya when one desires sight.
After having performed the introductory rite (upākaraṇa) and after having concluded the session (utsarga), one should observe a three-day period of suspension; some say a five-night period.
At the commencement and at the conclusion of the Vedas, [one should observe] the time-restriction.
Thus ends the fourth section.
The fifth section:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). ManGS_1,5.1 //

Having put on a garment made of darbha grass and having sipped water, he should mutter on the bank, "O grandson of the Waters," and then, having plunged into the water, [he should recite] "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, that [splendor] of Savitṛ."
With darbha grass in his hand, he recites the Sāvitrī three times and the first three sections (anuvākas) of the Veda.

“O divine waters, full of oblations, you are these *nigrābhya*s; may there be the great protection of the three. You are the life-sustainer of Agni. O divine waters, O waters, O daughter of the waters, O divine waters, sweet for Agni—*svāhā*! “Night after night... (these eight verses); “The plants that come together from all sides...”; “May the fathers purify me...”; “I meditate upon the fire that increases prosperity...”; “With what [splendor] will he appear to us as a messenger?”—these three [verses]. (ManGS 1.5.5)
Having purified themselves with the mantra, "We choose that which is auspicious for our welfare," they discard their garments and gratify the teachers according to the rite for the ancestors.
The remainder is explained by the rules for the *śrāddha* ceremony. *Manava-Gṛhya-Sūtra* 1.5.7.
Thus ends the fifth section.
The sixth section:
Now, therefore, they set the fire in motion.
To the north of the village or in front of it, having prepared a sacrificial altar (vedi) in a pure place, one should establish the seven meters in the location of the Āhavanīya fire; then,
having dug a furrow in the shape of a Prauga in the location of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire and filled it with Kuśa grass or handfuls of Darbha grass as seats (viṣṭhara),
one should fill the mound (utkara) behind it with water.

Having carried forward the fire into the place of the Gārhapatya and having offered eight oblations with the verse "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ," he offers six oblations with the formulas "ṛkṣāmaye prayuje svāhā" and so forth, and the seventh with "viśvo devasya netuḥ. (ManGS 1.6.2)

Having prepared three bundles of sacrificial fuel-sticks for the oblations, they stand facing east before the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering and, preceded by the *Vyāhṛtis*, place them upon the edge of the sacrificial mound with the three sections of the *Āpo hi ṣṭhīya* hymns, each ending with the word *svāhā*.

Having sprinkled the parched grains (*kausitān*) with water, they cause the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing with the parched grains; they cause the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing with the parched grains. (ManGS 1.6.4)
Thus ends the sixth section in the Mānava [Upaniṣad]. //6//
The Seventh Section.
Now, those who are worthy of the Upaniṣads:

a religious student of good conduct, one who is intelligent, one who performs his duties, a giver of wealth, a beloved, or one seeking further knowledge of the sacred teachings. (Manava-Grihya-Sutra 1.7.1)
Those are the sacred bathing places (tīrtha) of Brahmā.
He takes a wife.
One should choose [a bride] under the asterisms Kṛttikā, Svāti, or the Pūrvas. ManGS_1,7.4 //
For the marriage ceremony, as well as for the wedding, one should choose the asterisms Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, or the Uttarās; or whatever else is declared auspicious.
There are five factors that bring about marriage: wealth, beauty, learning, wisdom, and kinship.

If he fails to obtain one [of these], he should bestow wealth; if he fails to obtain the second, beauty; if he fails to obtain the third, knowledge. And they debate whether a kinsman is superior to wisdom. ManGS_1,7.7 //

A maiden from Bandhumatī who has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, of the same caste, from a family with different *pravara* lineages, younger [in age], still a virgin (*nagnikā*), and excellent.

One should perform the *vijñāna* rite for her: she should bring eight clods of earth—a clod from a sacrificial altar, a clod from a place where *dūrvā* grass grows, a clod from a cow-dung heap, a clod from beneath a fruit-bearing tree, a clod from a cemetery, a clod from a path, and a clod from a field of barley. (ManGS 1.7.9)

Having placed [the seed] in a temple, he should then cause the girl to take it; if she should take a clod of earth from a cemetery, or a clod from a path, or a clod from a fallow field, he should not marry her.
He should marry her who is endowed with [virtue], according to the Brāhma or Śaulka rite.
Saying "a hundred," he should give a chariot or a pair of cattle.
Thus ends the seventh section.
In the eighth section:
one should prepare four seats to the west of the fire.

They sit down upon these seats: the giver sits in front facing west, the recipient behind him facing east, the bride to the north of the giver facing west, and the officiant to the south facing north.
In their midst, having first spread out cotton and darbha grass and having filled a bronze vessel with water containing unbroken grains, she gives it to him while he is not yet widowed.
In that regard, there is gold. (ManGS 1.8.4)
He announces the eight auspicious objects.
Having recited the auspicious verses, [the student] says, "I give; I accept," three times; then the father or the brother shall give her as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa.
He pours out handfuls containing gold with the words, "For wealth, thee! The giver says, "For the sons, thee! and the recipient pours it back to him.
Having exchanged [the roles] four times, he gives.

Having accepted the girl with the Sāvitra formula and with the words "To Prajāpati," he attaches the phrase "Who has given this to whom? to every [formula], up to the end of "O Desire, this is yours."
"Equal indeed are our intentions," they recite together from this point until the end of the section.

"O Śatakratu, Indra thrice filled the hole of the chariot, the hole of the nose-rope, and the hole of the yoke; he made Apālā, who had the skin of the sun. With this [verse], one should sprinkle the girl with that water from the bronze vessel.
Thus ends the eighth section. //8//
The ninth section:
There are six persons worthy of the honey-mixture (ṣaḍāryāḥ): the officiating priest, the teacher, the bridegroom, the king, the accomplished student (snātaka), and a friend. ManGS 1.9.1.
Or they may honor those who are not related to the occasion, provided it has been a full year since their death.
The officiating priests and the members of the assembly are selected at the outset.
"One whose father is living should not accept the arghya," so says the Śruti; or rather, he may accept it. Manava-Gṛhyasūtra 1.9.4.
Then they honor him.
Having brought curd and honey into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup and covering it with a larger one, they proceed beginning with the water for sipping (ācamanīya).

"You are the milking of Virāj; you are the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj; may the milking of the Padyā Virāj be prepared for me"—with these words he looks at each calf as it is being brought.
Having accepted the seat-grass with the Sāvitra formula, he mutters: "I, like the sun rising above those who are equal to me, step upon this [seat-grass], whoever would seek to harm me. (ManGS 1.9.8)
With the words, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom," the teacher consecrates the throne-seat.
With the words, "May no harm come to you," he draws a grass mat beneath his feet.
To her as she sits upon a seat, he recites each verse three times.
"No indeed, sir," he says; "Homage to the lineage of seers," thus the Śruti declares as he touches the arghya water.

Having washed his feet with water for the feet and having accepted the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with the Sāvitrī verse, he sets it down and pours it out, saying, "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the vessel; homage to Rudra who dwells in the vessel," and with a span of his hand,
he sprinkles [the mixture] all around, moving clockwise from each direction, placing it higher and higher.
With the three verses beginning "The winds are honeyed for the one who follows the cosmic order," he sprinkles [the water] three times from left to right with his finger, verse by verse.
With the words, "Thou art the underlayer of immortality," he spreads [the food] as an underlayer.
"Truth, fame, and fortune—may Fortune resort to me! With this, he consumes the honey-mixture three times.
With the words, "Thou art the covering of immortality," he sips water.
He gives what remains to a friend.
With his hand on the sword, he says to the cow: *ManGS_1,9.19*.
"May my evil be struck down; may my evil be struck down! Om, do it!"—thus he issues the command.
He feeds four Brahmins belonging to different lineages.
One should have the Madhuparka prepared with either the limb of an animal or with milk-rice (pāyasa), for the sacred tradition states: "The Madhuparka is not meatless."

If she should release [the calf]—she who is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality—I shall speak for the sake of the wise person: "Do not harm the cow, do not harm the mother; do not strike Aditi. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! May she release it so that it may eat grass.
Now, you are an ornament that is not merely an ornament; may I become sufficient for everything.

"Quench my out-breath and in-breath; quench my upward-moving form. May I be well-eyed with my eyes, well-complexioned with my face, and may we be well-hearing with our ears"—with these words, he touches his limbs according to their respective characteristics, and then [puts on] two garments for the removal of odor.
I shall put on glory; I shall bestow glory. May I reach old age with long life.
May we live a hundred abundant autumns. I shall clothe myself in the nourishment of glory; may Heaven and Earth rejoice in my glory, as do Indra and Bṛhaspati.
"O worthy one, glory and fortune; let not my glory be taken away"—with these words, he puts on a new, unwashed garment.
At the pleasure-grove of the maiden, he sacrifices to Bhaga, Aryaman, Pūṣan, and Tvaṣṭṛ.
Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, four non-widowed women play joyful music.
Within the inner pavilion, he worships the wives of the gods.
Thus ends the ninth section. //9//
Tenth Section:

Having dug out a mark facing east-north, having sprinkled it with water, and having smeared the sacrificial mound with cow-dung, he should produce fire by friction and bring it forward facing [the sacrificer], whether the area be circular or square. Therein is the seating of the Brahman priest.

Having produced two strainers from Darbha grass with the appropriate mantra, having swept around the fire with the verse "This hymn for the worthy one," having sprinkled water around it, and having strewn grass around it, he spreads a single layer of grass outside the fire to the west.

Having drawn out the darbha grass with its tufts pointing eastward and northward, he spreads them out to the south and north of the fire, with the tips toward the fire, so that the northern blades lie upon the southern ones.

To the south of the fire, he spreads [grass] for the Brahman priest; further back for the sacrificer; behind that, at the midpoint, for the wife; and further back for the two water-vessels and the fried grains (lājās). Behind the pole-supporting beam, he places the two yoke-pins.

Having established her with the verse, "O Earth, be pleasant," and having fashioned pins from *śamī* wood, he places fire in the interior of the cow-pen and leads the wife forward while holding her hand.
Having grasped the hem of her garment with the mantra:

"Be not of fierce aspect, nor a bringer of enmity; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster; a mother of heroes, free from desire, and pleasant; be a source of welfare to us, to our bipeds, and to our quadrupeds," he leads her forward after encircling her, passing to the north of the chariot or the cart, walking around it, and crossing between the fire and the vehicle, placing her to the south of the northern draft-animal.

Having placed a maiden beneath the yoke-pole, having drawn out the pin (śamyā), and having interposed gold, he sprinkles her with water while reciting the three verses beginning "Golden-hued and pure," and then gives the command: "Make the sound of an arrow right here! ManGS 1.10.7.
Then he gives her the garment with [the verse]:
"Those who cut [it], those who spun [it], those who wove [it], those who brought [it] down,
and the divine women who stretched the edges all around upon the fire— "

"May those goddesses clothe you for long life; put on this long-lived garment"—having thus caused him to put on an unwashed garment, and having taken hold of him from behind, and having offered the two Āghāra and the two Ājyabhāga oblations, he offers on the northern half [of the fire] with "To Agni, the knower of people, svāhā!"; on the southern half with "To Soma, the knower of people, svāhā!";
and in the middle with "To Gandharva, the knower of people, svāhā! (ManGS 1.10.8).

Having yoked the fire with the two verses beginning with "yukto vaha yadākūtam," and having worshipped the lunar mansion, he should sacrifice to the deity of that lunar mansion, as well as to the deity of the lunar day (tithi) and the deity of the season (ṛtu).
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni.
And Agni gave me both Ravi and sons;
moreover, Agni Jātavedas was her first [husband].
May his wisdom release her from the noose of death;
may King Varuṇa grant his approval for this.
So that we may attain the triple-greatness of Indra through the power of Rudra—svāhā!
Thus, with the eight verses beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," he should offer oblations of clarified butter, one verse at a time.
With whatever rite one intends to cut [the hair], there one should offer the *jayā* oblations; and as for the *śruti* regarding those *jayā* oblations, it has been stated thus:
"To intent, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā!"
To Prayuja thee, svāhā! To Nabhas thee, svāhā!
To Aryamṇa thee, svāhā!
"For prosperity, svāhā to you! For victory, svāhā to you!
For desire, svāhā to you!"—and with this verse, he offers to Prajāpati and to the Stoma.
"Being pure, turn toward the west and look at her," he says.
While gazing at her, he mutters:
"May he place his heart in my vow; may your mind follow my mind;
with one-pointed mind, enjoy my speech; may Prajāpati yoke you to me. (ManGS 1.10.13)
"What is your name? and so forth. (ManGS 1.10.14)

When the name of the god has been proclaimed, [the officiant], while taking the hand, says: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take the hand of *so-and-so*. Facing eastward, standing upright, he takes the right hand of the girl—who is seated and facing westward—with his own right hand; it should be turned upward and held low, empty with an empty [hand]. Just as Indra, Savitṛ, Varuṇa, and Bhaga took her hand.
I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband.
Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi— the gods have granted you to me for the office of householder.
That speech which first spoke together before the gods and the Asuras—
that song we shall sing today, which is the highest mind of women.
O Sarasvatī, protect this [sacrifice], O auspicious one, rich in prizes!
You whom I, the breath of all that has been and all that is to be, lead forward at the beginning—there I am, not deluded;
there you are, not deluded; you are that, and I am that.
Heaven am I, you are the earth; you are the Ṛgveda, I am the Sāmaveda.
I am the seed; may you two bear the seed.
Let us two marry for the sake of bringing forth a male child, for the sake of glory and for the sake of producing a son.
For the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor.
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 1.10.15)
Having led them clockwise around [the fire], [he places them] behind the fire with [the mantra]:
"Mount this stone; like a stone, may you two become firm. May all the gods grant you a life-span of a hundred autumns."
Thus, with his two right feet, he causes [the boy] to step upon the stone.
Just as Indra descended from Gandhamādana together with Indrāṇī,
so may you descend from this stone together with your wife.
"Step up; may your feet be level. O maiden, may you be long-lived, possessed of sons.
Thus he causes her to step up twice.
He causes [the bride] to step around four times.
At each successive turn, [the officiant] should say, "May you two agree," and Brahmā should mutter the *brahmajapa*.
Thus ends the tenth section. //10//
Eleventh Section:
Thereafter, the assembly for the performance of the rite should be understood according to the specific requirements.
Having threshed and sprinkled either rice or barley for Aryaman, Agni, Pūṣan, and Varuṇa, he roasts them as parched grain (lājā).
He gives it to his mother, provided she has given birth to a son and is not a widow.
Then he gives her a second garment with that same mantra.
Having joined the two ends together with the formula, "The binding of Indra's wife with a Darbha cord," he ties a right-handed knot.

"I bind you together with the milk of the earth; I bind you together with the waters and the plants; I bind you together with offspring and wealth. Thus bound, press out the portion for the gods. With these words, she girds the girl with the yoke-tie from within her garment. (Manava Gṛhya Sūtra 1.11.6)
Then he prepares these: winnowing baskets, parched grains, stalks of grass, a stone, and collyrium.
With four blades of *darbha* grass or *śara* reeds, including their stalks and tufts, he rubs them against *traikakuba* ointment one by one, saying,
"Thou art the eye of Vṛtra," and thus anoints the right eye of the husband three times;
likewise the other [eye], and likewise that of the wife, with the remainder silently.
I pierce with the divining-sticks the eyes of those Rākṣasas who roam about in every direction as this bride approaches the presence of the fire; may the Lord of Beings grant well-being to the bride.
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 1.11.9)

Having placed the parched grains behind the fire, having mixed them with *śamī* leaves, and having divided them equally into four parts in a winnowing basket, he carries them around the front of the fire and hands them to the wife who holds the grains.
The brother or a celibate student pours parched grain from one joined palm into the other joined palms [of the bride].
With the under-spreading and the over-pouring of clarified butter, they two offer the *saṃpāta* oblation in an uninterrupted stream: "The maidens have worshipped the divine Aryaman Agni;
may that god Aryaman release us from here, and not from there—*svāhā*!"
For you, O Agni, they brought Sūryā away, together with her bridal procession.
Furthermore, O Agni, give the wife back to her husbands together with offspring.
Again Agni has given back the wife along with life and splendor;
may he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns.
"This woman, scattering fried grains into the fire, speaks thus:
'May my husband have a long life; may my kinsmen prosper. (ManGS 1.11.12)
Thus [he worships] the god Pūṣan and the god Varuṇa.
The oblations for marriage beginning with "yena dyaur ugrā," as well as the jaya, ābhyātāna, saṃtati, and rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings, [are performed]. (ManGS 1.11.14)
"Ākūtāya svāhā"—these are the *jayas*; "The eastern direction, the spring season"—these are the *abhyātānas*;
"From out-breath [I join] in-breath, making it continuous"—these are the *saṃtati-homas*; and "Truth, the sixfold, the abode of truth"—these are the twelve *rāṣṭrabhṛts*. (ManGS 1.11.15)
"Indra as the protector, and all the Ādityas"—this [is used] for auspicious occasions.
The parched grains are for Kāma; there is no fourth oblation for the sviṣṭakṛt. // ManGS_1,11.17 //

Then he causes her to take seven steps toward the east: "One for food, two for strength, three for progeny, four for the increase of wealth, five for well-being, six for the seasons—be a friend at the seventh step, O Sarasvatī, who art most gracious;
may thy wide expanse not be seen [by us]."
"May Viṣṇu lead you up"—this he joins on to every [formula].

To the west, on a red hide with the neck pointing eastward and the hairy side up, he spreads *darbha* grass; having spread it, he makes the bride sit upon it, or else directly upon the *darbha* grass itself.
I will loosen this noose of Varuṇa which Savitṛ, whose laws are true, has bound;
may he place me, uninjured, together with my husband in the womb of Dhātṛ, in the world of the well-performed deed.
Having thus fastened the cord-loop, he ties it at the end of the garment.
[He offers] with the two *anumati* [verses], with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with the two [mantras] beginning "And for us, O Agni... and "O Agni, thou who art not...". ManGS 1.11.21.
He places three fuel sticks made of Śamī wood, anointed with ghee, using these three verses ending with the word *svāhā*: "From the ocean with the waves... and so forth.
Having taken equal portions of unbroken barley meal and curds, and having offered with the mantra, "This oblation is procreative for me," he makes an additional offering of clarified butter.
They purify themselves with water from the pitcher while reciting the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
The bridegroom is the sacrificial fee. ManGS_1,11.27.
Thus ends the eleventh section. //11//
Twelfth Section: Auspicious is this bride; come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart from here.
Thus he addresses the spectators as they follow him.
At this very point, he performs the parting of the hair with a porcupine quill or a blade of Darbha grass together with its root, using the verse "O slayer of armies... (RV 10.103.12).
Then they anoint [her]: "Anointing her hair, being well-disposed, may you— possessing offspring, for the sake of glory, having many sons,
non-terrible, auspicious, and long-lived— be devoted to your husband, your father-in-law, and your mother-in-law."
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 1.12.3)
He unites her with a living woolen thread:
"Having gathered your hair—straight and not fierce—be a crest for all your friends.
Be auspicious when being carried by a noble family; be auspicious among the people and in the vehicles."
Thus [ends the section]. ManGS 1.12.4.
Then he causes them to eat curd and honey, or whatever may be fit for an oblation.
Having caused the benediction to be recited for him, they mutter together the verse, "Equal indeed are our intentions... and so forth.
Both eat together.
Thus ends the twelfth section. //12//
The thirteenth section:
On an auspicious day, he yokes [the cart].
With the two verses beginning "They harness the ruddy one," he consecrates the horse being harnessed, first the right side and then the left.
He cleanses the chariot with an unwashed garment or with *darbha* grass.

"Those who run toward the fire, having mounted the chariot with its two poles and yoke-pins, those winds that move about, whose weapon is far-reaching, winged, and powerful—may those fires of yours, being full, protect us. With these words he consecrates the wheels. "O Lord of the Forest, with strong limbs... with this [verse] he consecrates the seat. *Mānava Gṛhya Sūtra* 1.13.5.
O Sūryā, ascend the beautiful, white, all-formed Śalmalī tree, golden-hued, well-rolling, and with good wheels; go to the world of immortality and make it pleasant for your husband. Prepare yourself!
Thus he causes [the child] to ascend. (ManGS 1.13.6)
May the deities favor me; may Brahman favor my great heroism;
may the power that is in the nobility favor me, and may glory come to me today.
Having thus proceeded toward the east, he turns around to the right.
May the deities come toward me; may spiritual power, heroic vigor, sovereign dominion, whatever strength there is, and whatever glory there is, all come toward me.
Thus he addresses the sun as it is setting.
If he passes something inauspicious, he mutters: "May they give their consent. (ManGS 1,13.9)
"Salutation to Rudra, who dwells in the village," [he says] in the village; and also, "These [oblations] to Rudra. (ManGS 1.13.10)
"Salutation to Rudra, who dwells on the single tree," [he recites] at a single tree;
and also, "Those who are in the hollows of trees. (ManGS 1.13.11)
"In homage to Rudra, who dwells in the cremation ground," [he says] at the cremation ground;
and "Those who are the lords of beings. (ManGS 1.13.12)
At a crossroads, [he should offer with] "Homage to Rudra, who dwells at the crossroads," and also with "Those who guard the paths on the path. (ManGS 1.13.13)
At a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), [he should recite]: "Homage to Rudra, who dwells at the tīrtha," and also, "Those who wander among the tīrthas. (ManGS 1.13.14)
"Where the waters were to be crossed," [he says]. "Homage to the Ocean, the son of Veṇu, the lord of rivers!
Homage to the lord of all rivers!
May Viśvakarman always accept this oblation! Svarga! Svāhā!"—with these words, he pours handfuls of water into the water.
"I offer nectar into my mouth; may life and nectar enter my breath along with Brahman; he crosses over death.
Reciting "With power," "Safety," and "Liberation," while being released, he wipes his mouth three times and sips water, saying, "Drive away all fear, svāhā! ManGS 1.13.15.
If he crosses by boat, he should mutter the verse beginning with "sutrāmāṇam."

If the axle of the chariot, the yoke-pin, or any other part of the chariot should be damaged, one should kindle a fire right there, offer oblations with the *jaya* formulas and others, and mutter the verse: "This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold the bride. (ManGS 1.13.17)
Leap over the worn-out paths with speed; O Vaiśvānara, may you go before us with auspicious nourishment.
Whichever path the teacher travels, by that very path may we go together.
Thus, both of them depart.
They enter the village together with the cows at sunset, or according to the word of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the thirteenth section. //13//
On the fourteenth day, at the junction of the days, he should cause [the student] to enter the house.
Saying "To each Brahman," he descends.
Auspicious signs appear.
He spreads a continuous line of sacrificial grass from the cow-pen.
From the chariot, from the place of worship— those upon whom he relies when traveling abroad, and in whom there is great goodwill—
with them we call out; may they recognize us as having arrived.
Thus she assents. ManGS_1,14.5 //
I enter these houses with a joyful mind; for they are auspicious and kind to the hero among heroes.
Carrying nourishment and pouring forth clarity, may I dwell within them with a happy heart.
Having thus established the fires, he enters his dwelling together with his wife and the sacrificial implements, under the asterism Rohiṇī, Mūla, or whichever one is declared auspicious.

To the west of the fire, having spread Darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward upon the red hide of an ox, with the neck toward the front and the hair side up, he makes the bride sit upon it; or alternatively, he makes her sit upon the Darbha grass alone.
Then he causes this student of sacred knowledge to enter her lap:
"By Soma the Ādityas are strong; by Soma the earth is great;
in the lap of these stars, O such-and-such, Soma is established."
Thus [ends the section]. ManGS 1.14.8.
Then, having filled his joined palms with sesame seeds and rice mixed with fruit and having made him stand up, he should show her the smoke-ascending, living, and seven-sages [verses].
Infallible, steadfast, the wife of the Steadfast—may we behold her as firm in every way.
Steadfast are these mountains; steadfast is this woman in her husband’s family.
While she is looking on, he mutters this [formula]. *Manava Gṛhya Sūtra* 1.14.10.
On the following day, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of milk for Prajāpati, he offers it;
then, having added curds to the remainder of the clarified butter, he offers it with that remnant of the oblation.
"Like a chariot, like two oxen, may my speech go to you; let your mind come to me.
The union of the ruddy goose, that union has been made for us"—with these words, the sacrificer eats three times, and the wife eats what remains silently.
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is performed in the afternoon; it has been explained.
He who practices celibacy for a year, or for twelve nights, or for three nights, or for one night [is purified].
Then he should dismiss her to her own home.
Having applied the *yoktra* (cord), he should join them together:

"Beholding you with my mind as I meditate upon you, who were obstructing my own body at the proper season—come to me, O youthful woman, and rise up; be born, be born through offspring, O you who desire sons!"
O Prajāpati, take pleasure in my body; may Tvaṣṭṛ together with the gods, and Indra, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, make us the mothers of many sons.
I placed the embryo within the plants; I am within all existing worlds.
I brought forth the creatures upon the earth; I brought forth sons from their mothers in future times.
Thus he mutters the verse with the transposition of the words "woman" and so forth.
He touches [the child] with the formula, "May he do [it]. (ManGS 1.14.17)
"O mother"—this is the mantra for the birth ceremony.
"Bṛhat" is the established state of what has been born.
By this rite, he should cause [the couple] to unite during every fertile season.
Thus ends the fourteenth section. //14//
Fifteenth Section.

In the third month of pregnancy, having fetched the two kindling woods (araṇis) in the sixth or eighth month, and having offered oblations with the Jaya and following formulas, he causes the wife to sit on Darbha grass to the west of the fire; having loosened all her hair and anointed it with fresh butter, he parts her hair with a porcupine quill from a three-spotted one and a branch of Śamī wood with leaves, reciting: "Agni has given the wife back again. (ManGS 1.15.1)
Thus ends the fifteenth section. //15//
Sixteenth Section:

In the eighth month of pregnancy, having bathed [the woman] with *durvā* grass and fruits while reciting the *jaya* hymns and so forth, having covered her with an unwashed garment while reciting the section beginning with "yā oṣadhayaḥ," having adorned her with perfumes and flowers, and having tied fruits around her neck, [she should circumambulate] the fire clockwise.
He should perform [the rite]. (ManGS 1.16.1)
Having performed the worship with the mantra, "O hero, protect my offspring," he should feed virtuous Brāhmaṇas.
One should give fruits as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then follows the rite for well-being.
One should honor that teacher who is such.
Thus ends the sixteenth section. //16//
Seventeenth Section: When a son is born, he bestows a boon.
Having churned fire with two fire-sticks, he should offer oblations for long life into that fire.
With the section beginning "Thou art the life of Agni," he offers twenty-one oblations of clarified butter, verse by verse and in each successive turn.
Having touched curds, honey, and water with a piece of gold in the remnant of the clarified butter, he causes him to eat it three times.
Become a stone, become an axe, become uninjured gold; you are indeed the Veda, named "Son"—live for a hundred autumns!
Thus, with his handspan, he sprinkles [the water] over each part, facing it, moving clockwise, and from all sides.
Having wrapped the middle leaf of a *palāśa* tree around [the child's head], he should murmur over his two ears:

"Earth I give to thee" over the right ear; "Atmosphere I give to thee" over the left; "Heaven I give to thee" over the right; and "Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven I give to thee" over the left. (ManGS 1.17.6)
Saying, "Make food swell; make strength swell," he should cause the two breasts to be suckled.
Thus ends the seventeenth section. //17//
Eighteenth Section:

On the tenth night, one should give a name to the son—beginning with a sonant consonant, having a semivowel as its middle letter, consisting of two or four syllables; for daughters, it should consist of three syllables and end in a dental.

Therefore, having abandoned the father’s name for the purpose of salutation, he is forbidden from using a name that is based on a deity, based on a lunar mansion, or the actual name of a deity. Having bathed, he approaches together with his son.
Then he touches it with the formula: "With the brilliance of Agni, with the luster of Sūrya, with the power of all the gods, I touch you.
Having washed his hands, having anointed [the child] with fresh butter, and having warmed it over the fire, he should touch him after announcing it to a Brāhmaṇa; such is the Śruti. (ManGS 1.18.4)
He gives a boon to the performer.
You are born from limb after limb; you are produced from the heart. You are indeed the self named "son"; live for a hundred autumns.
Having returned from his journey, he should thus mutter over the head of his son.
One should not consume honey or meat until the animal sacrifice (Paśubandha).
And at the end of the year, one should sacrifice with a goat and a sheep to Agni and Dhanvantari.
Thus ends the eighteenth section. //18//
The nineteenth section:
Now, the viewing of the sun.
In the fourth month, having cooked a mess of boiled rice in milk, he offers an oblation of it.
"The bright Āditya has risen in the east; he is the one who dwells in the light when he goes toward this [world]. With these words, he offers an oblation to Sūrya.
Having performed the ritual salutation with the verse, "ud u tyam jātavedasam," he should show [the disciple] facing the sun, saying:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed One, possessor of a hundred rays, dispeller of darkness!
Destroy my misfortune, O God, and unite me with good fortune."
—thus [it is said]. (ManGS 1.19.4)
Now follows the libation for the Brahmins. *Manava-Grihya-Sutra* 1.19.5.
A bull is the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
The twentieth section:
Now follows the first feeding of solid food.

In the fifth or sixth month, having cooked a mess of rice in milk, having bathed and adorned the child and covered him with a new garment, and having offered an oblation with the mantra "O Lord of Food, give us food," he should make the child eat from [the vessel] with gold while reciting the verse: "From food, the flowing [nectar]... (RV 8.69.3).
One should display ornaments made of jewels and gold, as well as weapons.
If he so desires, he should accept that.
Then follows the feeding of the Brahmins.
A garment is the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the twentieth section. //20//
The twenty-first section:
When the greater part of the third year has passed, one should have the tonsure (cūḍā) performed.
During the northern course of the sun, under a bright lunar fortnight, and under an auspicious constellation, except for the nine [asterisms].
Having offered the *jaya* and other oblations,
[he recites]: "With warm water, may Vāyu, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa bestow long life upon the sacrificer who offers."
Thus he consecrates the warm water with a mantra.
May Aditi shave the hair; may the waters flow forth for life;
may Prajāpati sustain it again and again for well-being.
Thus he overflows. (ManGS 1.21.3)
With the words, "O herb, protect her," he places a blade of darbha grass between [the hair and the razor] at this southern parting of the hair.
With the words, "O Svadhiti, do not harm him," he places the razor down.
With that razor wherewith Savitṛ shaved the hair of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that let the Brāhmaṇa shave him; may he be long-lived and reach old age.
With that by which Pūṣan shaved Bṛhaspati for the sake of sensory power and long life,
with that I shave you for long life, for the sake of living a long life.
With that whereby this sun moves further and beholds for long,
with that I besmear you for the sake of life, for fair renown, and for well-being.
Thus, with these three verses, he sows three times.
As you, O barber, shave the hair with a sharp-edged razor of great luster, purify the head; do not diminish his lifespan.
Thus he hands over the razor made of iron for the shaving of the hair.
May this luster not follow after your hair; may the Creator (Dhātṛ) establish it for you accordingly.
For you, Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ have bestowed luster.
Thus he recites the consecratory formula over [the hair] as it is being shaved.
He collects a handful of green cow-dung from a friend.
Having shaved the hair of King Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and Agni—
finding no great place of concealment for them— sought it within the space between heaven and earth.
Thus he recites the mantra over them as they are being carried toward the north-east.
"One should cause her to join [the grains] while she is not empty-handed"—thus says the Śruti.
He gives a choice gift to the performer, and a ball of wool and black sesame seeds to the barber who shaves his hair.

According to this procedure, in the sixteenth year, for one who is about to undergo the Godāna ceremony or to kindle the sacred fire, the fire is called the *godānika* or *maitrāyaṇi*; such is the Vedic revelation.
With the words, "May Aditi shave the beard," he shaves the beard with a razor, and with the words, "Cleanse the face."
Thus ends the twenty-first section. //21//
The twenty-second section:
the presentation of the gift occurs on the seventh or ninth day.
We have come together as arrivals; may he ward off our first affliction. May we move about unharmed, traversing the quarters with well-being, and returning home in safety.
Having thus had his hair shorn, bathed, anointed with oil, massaged with ointment, adorned, and wearing the sacrificial cord, he comes together and mutters [the following].
Then he gives him a garment [with the verse]: "Those goddesses who cut it, those who spun it, those who wove it, those who brought it,
and those divine ones who stretched the ends all around— may they clothe you."
May those goddesses clothe you for old age; O long-lived one, put on this garment.

Having caused him to put on an unwashed garment and having taken hold of him, he offers the two Āghāra and two Ājyabhāga oblations; then, having brought curds into the remnants of the sacrifice, he consumes the curds three times with the mantra: "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan. (ManGS 1.22.3)
"Who are you by name? he asks. (ManGS 1.22.4)

When the name has been announced, [the teacher], while taking the hand, says: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand, O so-and-so. He takes the hand of one who is facing east while facing west; standing while [the student] is seated; the right [hand] which is turned upward with the right [hand] which is turned downward; with an empty [hand] he takes [the hand] with an empty [hand]. "Savitṛ took your hand, O so-and-so; Agni is your teacher."
O God Savitṛ, this student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) has returned; protect him.
Whose student of sacred knowledge are you?
You are the student of sacred knowledge of Prāṇa.
Who leads you to whom?
To whom do I entrust you? For whom do I entrust you?
I entrust you to him; I entrust you to Bhaga; I entrust you to Aryaman; I entrust you to Savitṛ; I entrust you to Sarasvatī;
I entrust you to Indra and Agni; I entrust you to the Viśve Devas; I entrust you to all.
"I entrust [him] to the gods," with these words he entrusts him.
"Thou art the knot of Brahmā; may it not loosen for thee," with these words he mutters while beginning at the region of the heart.
"Thou art the knot of the vital breaths," [he mutters] over the region of the breaths. (ManGS 1.22.6)

Guardian of the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), overcomer of heat, slaying the demon and subduing the enemies—come hither to us from every side; O auspicious, blessed girdle, may we not suffer harm through you, our sustainer.
Thus he takes up the girdle made of muñja grass, which is threefold and represents the earth.
With the verse, "Young and well-clad," he thrice winds the girdle around her from left to right.
It binds the knots of the man and the woman.
"Driving away ill-spoken words, purifying our ancient luster, she has come to us;
bestowing strength through the out-breath and in-breath—may we not suffer harm, O auspicious goddess, O blessed girdle!
Thus he mutters when it has been tied around him.
May he place your heart in my vow; may your mind follow my mind; with single-minded devotion, enjoy my word; may Bṛhaspati bind you to me.
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 1.22.10)
Having given him a staff made of a sacrificial tree and a black antelope skin, he causes him to worship the sun:
"O Lord of the paths, may I attain the excellence of the journey and reach the end of this path.
May that eye, established by the gods, the bright one, rise in the east."
May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns;
may we hear for a hundred autumns; may we speak for a hundred autumns;
may we remain undaunted for a hundred autumns, and even more than a hundred autumns.
May that wisdom which is among the Apsarases and that mind which is among the Gandharvas—
may that divine and human wisdom enter into me right here.
Thus [ends] ManGS 1.22.11.
Having led him clockwise around [the fire], he places him behind the fire [with the words]:
"Come, mount this stone; like a stone, may you be firm.
May all the gods grant you a life of a hundred autumns."
Thus, with his right foot, he causes him to step upon a stone.

To the west of the fire, having spread out a large mat and made it well-levelled, he sits facing east and causes [the student], who is seated facing west, to recite the Gāyatrī verse dedicated to Savitṛ; for some also [cause him to recite] the Triṣṭubh, and others the Jagatī; [he recites them] with the syllable *om*, with the word *apaḥ* (water), and with the Vyāhṛtis.
He should hold it [the vessel] three times; having cut it twice, he should pour it out once, by quarters, by half-verses, and finally the whole with the end [of the verse].

"Whatever he recites in the morning for three [verses], for two, or for one—whether in a year, on a twelve-day period, a six-day period, or a three-day period—for that reason it is said in the Śruti: 'Therefore, they should be recited all at once.'"
He gives a brass vessel and a garment to the performer of the rite.
But for one who desires intelligence, having anointed a *palāśa* leaf with fresh butter, he should have him recite [this] in its shade: "O you of good fame, you are of good fame!
Just as you, O you of good fame, are of good fame, so make me, O you of good fame, possessed of good fame."
Just as you are the guardian of the treasures of the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasures of the Vedas for human beings.
Thus [ends] ManGS 1.22.17.
"Or rather, he who initiates one who knows this follows one, two, three, or all of these Vedas"—so says the Śruti.
The student life (*brahmacarya*) has been explained. *Manava-Grihya-Sutra* 1.22.19.
Then, when he goes for alms, he should first approach his mother, and then any other female relatives who may be present.
"He prepares alms for the teacher; when permitted by him, he may eat"—so says the Śruti.
Thus ends the twenty-second section.
The twenty-third section:
Now follows the initiation based on the fourfold [Veda], lasting for one year.
He should offer the Caturhotṛ formulas pertaining to his own ritual act, together with the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ and the Saptahotṛ.
Finally, having administered the vow, he should cause [the student] to recite the first two sections (anuvākas).
In this very manner, one should perform the *uddīkṣā* oblation.
Now follows the twelve-night rite pertaining to the initiation fire.

Having offered the eight verses beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manaḥ," he offers six oblations with the formula "akūtam agniṃ prayuñjan svāhā," and the seventh with "viśvo devasya netuḥ. (ManGS 1.23.6)
Having first given him the vow, he should cause him to recite six sections (anuvākas).
He should fetch water three times a day, three jars at each occasion.
He should sleep on the ground covered with a single garment, or on ashes, dried cow-dung, or sand.
One should not descend into water.
When [the study] is completed, having sacrificed with an oblation of cakes mixed with ghee, he should cause the Vātsa [hymn] to be recited.
Then one should feed the Brahmins with cakes mixed with ghee.
In this very manner, one should offer the Uddīkṣā oblation.
Now, the initiation for the Aśvamedha lasts for eleven nights.

Having added fuel of vetasa wood and having offered oblations with the ninth Anuvāka, he should worship with the sixth [Anuvāka], give the vow-food, and cause him to recite twenty-one Anuvākas starting from the beginning.
Three times a day he should bring fodder for the horse, three handfuls each time.
He should sleep on the ground covered with a single garment, or on ashes, cow-dung, or sand.

Having consecrated water with the four sections beginning with "The herbs that come together" (*yā oṣadhayaḥ samānyāyanti*), "May the fathers purify me" (*punantu mā pitaraḥ*), and "In accordance with the mind of Agni" (*agnermanvā*), he should perform his bath.
In this very manner, one should offer the Uddīkṣā oblation.
He should cause [the student] to recite the fourteen sections beginning with "śādaṃ dadbhiḥ."
When about to request instruction in the secret portion, he [requests] the Pravargya.
Regarding the instruction, it is as previously explained.
He should cause him to recite twenty-five sections from the beginning.
This is explained by the same procedure as the initiation for those who have mastered the three Vedas.
At the beginning, he should cause him to recite three sections (anuvākas).
The vows have been explained; the vows have been explained. // ManGS_1,23.26 //
With the words, "The highest bond of Varuṇa," he unfastens the girdle.
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the Maitrāyaṇīya-Mānava-Gṛhya; the first chapter is completed.
The presentation of the gift occurs on either the seventh or the ninth day. //1//
We have come together as arrivals; may he ward off our first affliction. May we move about unharmed; may we travel safely in every direction. May there be well-being from the seizers.
Having thus had his hair shorn, bathed, anointed with oil, massaged, adorned, and wearing the sacred thread, he approaches and mutters [the following].
1–22–2) Then he gives him the garment itself: "Those who cut it, those who spun it, those who wove it, and those who brought it;
and the divine women (*gnās*) who stretched the borders all around."
May those goddesses clothe you in old age; long-lived, put on this garment.
This is the unwashed garment.
(1-22-6-7-8-9) This goddess has come to us, driving away evil speech and purifying our ancient luster;
bestowing strength through the out-breath and in-breath, may she, the auspicious goddess, the fortunate girdle, protect us, O noble one.
When she has been girt with the sacrificial cord, he recites:
"May he place your heart in my vow; may your mind follow my mind; enjoy my word with single-minded devotion; may Bṛhaspati join you to me."
Thus [ends verse 10].

Having given him a staff of a tree suitable for sacrifice and a black antelope skin, he causes him to worship the sun with this verse: "O Lord of the Path, may I reach the end of this auspicious path, the best of paths.
May that bright eye, ordained by the gods, rise up before me."
May we hear for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns;
may we remain undaunted for a hundred autumns, and even longer than a hundred autumns.
That wisdom which is among the Apsarases, that mind which is among the Gandharvas, and that divine as well as human wisdom— may it enter into me right here.
Thus [ends the eleventh verse].
Having led him around to the right, [the teacher] stands behind the fire and says:
"Come, step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm.
May all the gods grant you a hundred autumns of life."
(Thus, with his right foot, he causes him to step upon a stone. //12//

To the west of the fire, having spread out a large mat and made it well-levelled, sitting facing east, he causes [the student], who is sitting facing west, to recite the Gāyatrī Sāvitrī—some indeed [cause him to recite] the Triṣṭubh, some the Jagatī—after saying "Om," and with the Vyāhṛtis. 13.
One should hold it down three times; having cut it off twice, one should join it once—by foot, by half-verse, and finally the whole verse with its end.

Because [the *sāmidhenī* verses] are recited in three ways—over three days, over two days, or over one day; over a year, twelve days, six days, or three days—the Śruti declares that they are to be recited all at once (*sadyas*). //15//
He gives a bell-metal vessel and a garment to the performer of the rite. //16//
But for one who desires intelligence, having anointed a *palāśa* leaf with fresh butter, he should have [the student] recite over its shadow:
"O you of good fame, you are of good fame;
as you, O you of good fame, are of good fame, so make me, O you of good fame, possessed of good fame."
"Just as you are the guardian of the treasures of the Vedas for the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasures of the Vedas for human beings. //17//
"He studies here one, two, three, or all of these Vedas; he who initiates this learned man follows him"—such is the Śruti. //18//
The practice of celibacy has been explained. //19//
Then, when he goes out for alms, he should first approach his mother, and then any other female friends who may be present. //20//
"He prepares alms for the teacher; with his permission, he may eat"—such is the sacred tradition (śruti). //21//
The second [topic] concerns the person: the father of the deceased should establish the domestic fire (śālāgni) for the wedding. ManGS 2.1.1.

Except for that [case], when the father has died, they should keep the fire burning and remain awake on a festival day, during the full moon, under an auspicious lunar mansion, except on the ninth day.
Having bathed, being pure, and wearing unwashed garments.
Restraining my speech, I shall remain awake until dawn.
In an open space, having ground unhusked barley, he mixes a thick mash with a stalk of sugarcane, without using a stirring-stick.
We invoke Savitṛ of the golden hands, Vāyu, Indra, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, and the Aṅgirasas;
may they pacify that flesh-eating Agni.
Thus he sprinkles the fire with the churning-stick.
May King Soma distribute [the portions]; may Agni, while distributing, [place him] here. Let Agni be the bearer of the oblation; drive away the flesh-eater.
Having thus placed the fire upon the prepared mat, he sends it forth.
I send the flesh-eating fire far away; let it go to the kingdom of Yama, carrying off impurities.
Let this other Jātavedas remain right here, knowing well, to carry the oblations to the gods.
Having thus taken up the fire, they carry it toward the south-west.
They go together with their legal disputes.
Upon our own desert,
upon the head of the thieves, upon the pillow of the head,
and upon the black woolen garment— having wiped it off, O bounteous ones, let the dead go to their rest.
Thus, having placed lead upon it, he places [the other substances] one upon the other.
With the three verses beginning "From every abode," they cleanse themselves outside the cow-pen.
They return without looking back.
With reeds or with a branch of cane, they erase the footprints—erasing the footprints of death while extending this long life.
May they, swelling with offspring and wealth, become pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice. (ManGS 2.1.13)
"Grasp the ox that draws the boat, by which Saramā, crying out, was made to tremble."
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 2.1.14)

Having dug up the site for the fire-altar and sprinkled it with water, he pours out the terrestrial materials required for the establishment of the sacred fires, with the exception of saline soil and sand.
Having churned fire from two kindling sticks and having placed a fragment of gold [in it], he establishes the blazing fire before sunrise while sitting in the *upastha* posture, saying "Bhūḥ."
A cow, a garment, and bell-metal are the sacrificial fees.
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter.
The second section:

Having drawn the lines toward the east and north, sprinkled [the ground], and smeared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with cow dung—whether circular or square—one should produce fire by friction and bring it forward facing oneself. ManGS_2,2.1 //
Having prepared two strainers of darbha grass with the appropriate mantra, he cooks the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni.
When the purifier has been removed, having poured water and added rice grains, he cooks the rice while stirring it clockwise with a stirring-ladle, so that it remains alive.
Having poured clarified butter that has not been strained, or fresh butter that has been strained, over the cooked food, he removes it to the north.

Having swept around the fire with the words "This hymn for the worthy one," having sprinkled water around it, and having strewn grass around it, he spreads a single layer of sacrificial grass behind the fire.

Having drawn out the darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward, he spreads it out to the south and to the north of the fire, with the southern blades placed underneath the northern ones.
To the south of the fire, he spreads [grass] for the Brāhmaṇa; further [to the south], for the sacrificer; and in the western half, for the wife.

Having washed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) on the northward-spread sacrificial grass (*pavitra*), he places two of each upon that which has been spread.

Having silently poured out the clarified butter (ājya) to the south, having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagni-karaṇa) according to the mantra, and having silently wiped the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), the wife gazes at the clarified butter, saying: "I gaze upon thee with unimpaired vision.
Having silently placed it on the fire, then removed it from the fire, and set it down behind the fire, she purifies it with a mantra and gazes at it.
The sacrificer looks at the clarified butter with the mantra, "Thou art splendor."
Having placed the dipping-spoon (sruva) in the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), he places the sacrificial porridge (sthālīpāka) in front of it, and the stirring-stick (mekṣaṇa) behind it.

Having silently placed the fuel-stick facing eastward and addressed the Brahman priest, when told "Oṃ, offer!", he, sitting facing east between his knees with his right hand, offers the two Āghāra libations: the one for Prajāpati in the northern half, directed eastward, mentally; and the one for Indra in the southern half, likewise directed eastward. (ManGS 2.2.13)
Then he offers the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*): the portion for Agni in the northern half [of the fire] and that for Soma in the southern half, making them equal in size.

Having yoked the fire with the two verses beginning "Yukto vaha yadākūtam," he should worship the lunar mansion and sacrifice to the deity of that mansion; likewise, he should sacrifice to the lunar day and its deity, and to the season and its deity. (ManGS 2.2.15)

Having spread [the under-layer of ghee] and touched water, he cuts portions from the cooked rice with the stirring-spoon: from the middle, a second from the eastern half, and a third from the western half, if it is for an offering of five cuttings.
Having offered the portion cut off, he pours clarified butter over the cooked rice in the pot.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—with these words he offers in the center.
"Yo devānām asi" is for [the offering] to Rudra.
Having offered the Jaya oblations, he cuts a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half of the *ājya* once, measuring two finger-breadths;
or twice, if it is a five-fold cutting.
Having poured out [the portion] and sprinkled clarified butter over it twice, he does not sprinkle clarified butter over the sthālīpāka again after this point.
With the formula, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! he offers [the oblation] without letting it touch the previous one, in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire].

Having placed the stirring-spoon and the *darbha* grass blades [on the altar], he should offer oblations with the two *anumati* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, and with these [mantras]: "O Agni, you are ours," "So you are ours, O Agni," and "And you are the Unerring One, O Agni. (ManGS 2.2.23)
Having recited, "I loosen thy cord, I loosen thy reins," and having thrown the two strainers after [the oblation], he makes an offering over them with clarified butter.
"Thou art fuel; may we prosper," with these words he places a piece of wood on the fire; "Thou art kindling; may we thrive," with these words he places a second one.
With the mantra, "Today I have entered the waters," he worships [the water].
He should perform the ritual sprinkling with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha."
A full vessel is the sacrificial fee.
He offers the feather of a peacock. ManGS_2,2.29.
By this [description of] the *sthālīpāka*, all *sthālīpākas* are explained.
Thus ends the second section in the second chapter. //2//
The third section:
"To Agni, svāhā!"—with these words he offers in the evening; "To Prajāpati," with these words he offers the second oblation. (ManGS 2.3.1)
"To Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus at dawn; "To Prajāpati," he says for the second [offering].

There is a *sthālīpāka* for Agni and Soma on the full moon day, one for Indra and Agni on the new moon day, and an offering to Agni on both occasions; the guest-offering comes first on the full moon day, and the latter on the new moon day.
On the morning of the full moon day of Āśvayuja, he causes a sthālīpāka to be brought in connection with the regular sthālīpākas.
He sacrifices to Agni, Rudra, Paśupati, Īśāna, Tryambaka, Śarava, Praṣātaka, and the Cows.

Having offered curd-mixture mixed with curds and clarified butter with the verses "pra ṣātakaḥ," "tasyā naḥ," and "mitrāvaruṇā pravāha," he causes the cows to eat water with the formula, "Ambhaḥ stha, ambho vo bhakṣīya."
And once released, they may dwell [there].
One should feed the Brahmins with ghee.
One should not eat of the new grain without having performed the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
At the [proper] festival time, one should perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice with barley in the spring and with rice in the autumn.
Having cooked a pot-offering (sthālīpāka) in milk from the first-fruits, he offers of it with the formulas: "In unison with Heaven and Earth, svāhā! In unison with Soma, svāhā! (ManGS 2.3.11).
In autumn, he offers śyāmāka grains for Soma; in spring, he offers bamboo-yeast (veṇuyava) grains; in both cases, the oblation is accompanied by ghee.
The sacrificial fee is a first-born calf.
"A Brāhmaṇa alone should eat the remainder of the sacrificial oblation," so says the Śruti.
Thus ends the third section regarding the second person. //3//
The fourth section:
One who is about to sacrifice with an animal performs the service of the fire according to the procedure of the *pākayajña*.
It is performed silently like the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), with the exception of the ritual formulas (āvṛt) and the oblation to the deities. 2.4.2.

Having sprinkled [the animal] with water, having obtained its consent, having given it water to drink, having carried fire around it, and having established the *śāmitra* fire, they follow him as he steps northward while holding the two *vapāśrapaṇī* spits.
He gazes at it while it is being appeased.

Having addressed [the victim] and bathed it, having extracted the omentum according to the respective deity and cooked it, and having offered the two *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* oblations, he offers the omentum with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, go to the gods with the omentum; for you have become the first Hotṛ.
O Agni, be united with your body through the clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true—Svāhā!
Thus he offers the omentum. (ManGS 2.4.5)
"svāhā svāhā"—these two are for the scattering of the grains.
He causes the cooked rice from the pot to be brought forward, having the same deity as the animal sacrifice.
In that case, the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) are performed with the dhuvā-spoon.
The Sviṣṭakṛt offering is unexpressed.

Having taken a portion of the essence from the sacrificial portions of the animal sacrifice (*pāśubandha*), and having performed the offerings to the deities, he conquers the quarters with the remainder of the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*), just as he does for the *vanaspati* with the whey (*vājina*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having offered the *jayā* oblations, he cuts off portions from three limbs for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
The remainder is explained by [the rules for] the *sthālīpāka* offering. *Manava-Gṛhya-Sūtra* 2.4.12.
For an animal sacrifice, the sacrificial fee is indeed an animal.
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter. //4//
Fifth Section:
The Raudra Śūlagava sacrifice is performed in autumn.
In the north-eastern direction, near the village, at night, a sacrificial post (yūpa) is fashioned in the midst of cows.

Before the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, one should offer eight vessels of blood in the cardinal and intermediate directions with the eight Anuvākas beginning with "Obeisance to thee, O Rudra, in thy wrath" (namas te rudra manyave). ManGS_2.5.3.
One should not fetch water from a village that has not been drawn up.
The remainder, including even the skin, he should bury in the ground.
They say that for the animal sacrifices of the *pākayajña* rites, there are many sacrificial posts (*yūpa*).
Thus ends the fifth section in the second chapter. //5//
Sixth Section:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Dhruva horse.
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja.
The officiating priest shall be free from physical defects, bathed, pure, and wearing unwashed garments.
Before sunset, having gone out to the north of the village or to the east, in a pure place beneath an *aśvattha* or a *nyagrodha* tree,
or near water, one should prepare an altar-shaped mound. Upon it, there should be a four-cornered branch of a tree, free from cloth, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
with water-pots placed in the four directions along with boxes containing gold and seeds, and provided with cakes, straw mats, parched grain, *ullopikā* sweets, auspicious fruits, and dice.

Having prepared all kinds of perfumes, all kinds of flavors, all medicinal herbs, and all types of jewels, and having set up the fire upon a site adorned with *pratisara*, *dadhi*, honey, sweetmeats, *svastika*, and *nandyāvarta* designs, and having arranged fuel from any one of the *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *rohitaka*, or *udumbara* trees, he sacrifices to the three principal deities— Uccaiḥśravas, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu— with cooked messes of rice (*sthālīpāka*), and to the two Aśvins with animal victims.
And on the two days of Āśvayuja, [he offers] clarified butter.

Having offered the Jaya oblations, he consecrates the water with the four Anuvākas beginning with "The plants that grow together" (*yā oṣadhayaḥ saṃmanya-yanti*) and "May the Fathers purify me" (*punantu mā pitaraḥ*) and "From the mind of Agni" (*agnermanve*), and then bathes the horses.
Having adorned it with garlands of perfumes, they circumambulate the sacrificial ground three times, keeping it to their right.
They cause [the bride] to rejoice.
When the sacrifice is completed, they go to their respective places.
A white bull is the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the sixth section in the second chapter.
The seventh section:
On the full moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in milk, he offers of it with [the verse]: "O waters, you who were seized by the white-footed one in the east and in the west..."
And these seven offspring of Varuṇa, and all those who are kinsmen of the King—svāhā!
The white horse, the ruddy one, bestows [life]; the stallion, long enduring, impregnates the swift-moving womb.
Like people clothed in garments, they move together; you are the manifestor of all this.
Hail to the white, howling dog!
Indeed, in the transgression against the white one, no serpent has ever killed anything.
Hail to the white Vaitāhavya!
May there be safety for us from those belonging to Prajāpati; Svāhā!
Thus [ends the section]. (ManGS 2.7.1)

Having spread an unwashed garment with its fringes pointing north upon the bed, he pours water upon rice or barley grains placed there, [reciting] the two verses beginning with "Be a pleasant earth" (*syonā pṛthivī bhava*) and the two verses beginning with "The good protector" (*sutrāmāṇam*).

Then, with a branch of the *śamī* tree together with its leaves, he wipes upwards three times, [reciting] the two verses beginning with "Be a pleasant earth" (*syonā pṛthivī bhava*), the two verses beginning with "The good protector" (*sutrāmāṇam*), and the three verses beginning with "Homage be to the serpents" (*namo astu sarpebhyaḥ*).
May the serpents be appeased; may they go to their own resting places—those who dwell in the intermediate space and those who are stationed in heaven.
Let us descend upon this great earth, which is auspicious, eternal, gracious, peaceful, and blessed with a good winter; may we perform this rite year after year.
Thus he causes the eldest to enter first, moving from west to east.

"Long has the life-breath of the living one come; the night has passed away and light approaches. She has opened the path for the sun to travel; we have come where our lifespan extends further. Thus they emerge, with the youngest going first.
On the full moon day of Caitra, [the rite of] udgrahaṇa [is performed].
In that case, there is no cooked rice offering (stālīpāka), nor does one wipe [the vessel] with a branch.
This bed is the furtherer of riches; may this bed bring us across all difficulties. May we live long, with all our heroes unharmed.
Thus the bed is consecrated with this mantra. (ManGS 2.7.8)
The three [sacrifices] are performed on the full moon days of Phālguna, Āṣāḍha, and Kārttika.
One should not study while those [sounds] are present.
In those [waters], a pot-cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) is prepared in milk; that has been explained.
Thus ends the seventh section in the second chapter.
Eighth Section:
There are three Aṣṭakās.
From after the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa until before the full moon of Phālguna, these are the eighth days of the mixed fortnights.
One should not study while those [sounds] are present.
Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) in milk over those [fires], he offers of it:
"O Goddess who art most excellent among the *aṣṭakās*, who art heat-removing and heat-expelling;
you are the expeller of Varuṇa in the sacrifice; with this we shall worship you."
The mortars and the pressing-stones have raised their voice, preparing the oblation for the year-long rite.
O Ekāṣṭakā, may we live long with good offspring and brave sons, bringing tribute to you.
The night which people greet with joy as she approaches like a cow,
she who is the mistress of the year— may she be auspicious to us.
O Night, who art the image of the year, for those who worship thee,
grant offspring endowed with long life, and unite them with the abundance of wealth.
Thus are the four [offerings] of the *sthālīpāka*. (ManGS 2.8.4)
At every [offering], he appends: "To Aṣṭakā, for the one who bestows wealth, svāhā!"

May the winter, spring, and summer seasons be auspicious to us; may the rainy season be auspicious and free from fear for us for a long time. May Vaiśvānara, our supreme support and provider of vital breath, and day and night grant us a long life.

Peaceful be the earth, auspicious the mid-air; may the divine heaven grant us fearlessness. Auspicious be the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the sub-quarters for us; may the waters and the lightnings protect our life.

May the waters and the rays protect me on every side; may Dhātṛ and the ocean grant me fearlessness. May the past and the future be auspicious for me, as I guard my own voice through the praise of the Brahman.
May the poet Agni, Indra, Soma, Sūrya, and Vāyu be mine; may Agni Vaiśvānara drive away evil. May Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ grant protection; may Pūṣan bestow upon me prosperity and sovereign splendor.
