Thus [is the procedure] for the five [oblations] of clarified butter. (ManGS 2.8.6)
Having offered the Jaya oblations, he says, "O Agni, eat the iḍā," and [performs] the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Thus for all [the rites]. (ManGS 2.8.8)
Thus ends the eighth section in the second chapter.
Ninth Section:
At nightfall on the ninth day, one should have an image of a cow made out of clay at a crossroads.
Whoever should come, to each of them he should give [it]. (ManGS 2.9.2)
On the following day, he should have another [fire] established.
He should offer the omentum for it with [the verse]:
"Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors, wherever you know them to be placed in the distance; let streams of fat and ghee flow forth; may the desires of the sacrificer come true—svāhā!
Then he cooks rice porridge with milk on her breast.
The remainder of the ritual for him is explained by the procedure for the Aṣṭakā oblation.
He cooks the remaining portion of the food.
On the following day, having cooked the remaining food, he places three balls of meat-rice according to the procedure for the rice-balls.
One should offer the ancestral oblation (śrāddha) to the ancestors during the latter fortnight of the month.
"One should feed the Brahmins well-protected food; one should not eat what is not known through the Veda"—so says the Śruti.

If he should perform it with a cow or another animal, there shall be the sprinkling with water, the leading forward, the carrying of fire around, the taking of the firebrand, and the offering of the omentum. (ManGS 2.9.11)
One should offer the omentum, the cooked rice from the pot, and the portions of the sacrificial food three times each.

He offers the first oblation with the formula: "To Soma, accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! The second with: "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! The third with: "To Agni, the bearer of the Kavyas, svadhā! Adoration! (ManGS 2.9.13).
In this manner, the ritual procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is to be performed regularly month after month.
Thus ends the ninth section of the second [chapter]. //9//
Tenth Section:
On the full moon day of Phālguna, one should first worship Bhaga and Aryaman with fried grains and cakes.

Having ground the sacrificial grains for Indrāṇī, having purified the flour, and having cooked as many pairs of figures as there are species of animals, and having placed them in a bronze vessel with clarified butter, he offers it with the formula: "Svāhā to Rudra," or, according to some, "to Īśāna."
In the evening, he proceeds with two cakes for Agni and Indra.
The Āgneya is Tundila; his wives do not eat [the sacrificial food], whereas those of the other [the Vaidhasa] do, along with all the ministers.
With the cooked rice from the pot, he should sacrifice to Indrāṇī or to Śavī.

In the case of multiple assemblies, there is a single layer of sacrificial grass (barhis), and the Āghāra, the two Ājyabhāga portions, the clarified-butter oblations, and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering are likewise single.
With these [deities]— Agni, Indra, Soma, Sītā, Savitṛ, Sarasvatī, Citrā, Anumati, Revatī, Rākā, Pūṣan, and Rudra—

one worships these deities at the ploughing, the driving around, the sowing, the gathering of clods, the furrow-sacrifice, the threshing-floor sacrifice, the lute-sacrifice, and the ox-sacrifice, as well as during the seasonal festivals throughout the year.
In rivers, oceans, wells, and ponds, he sacrifices to Varuṇa; in herbs and trees, to Soma; and in those [objects] for which no deity has been specifically prescribed, to Agni.
Thus ends the tenth section of the second [chapter].
The eleventh section: The conclusion is even and with its root. (ManGS 2.11.1)
For one desiring food, [the ground] should slope toward the south; the offspring born there will be prone to consumption.
Flowing equally from all sides.
Or else, one should choose a place where the waters flow from the north-east after converging.
Or else, it may be filled with dust by those who are careful after having dug a pit.

"Here I enclose this house for the sake of offspring, food, splendor, and Vedic luster," with these words he encloses the house; having placed gold in a pit, he offers an oblation with the formula: "To the unshakable, the firm, the terrestrial, Svāhā!
He worships it with the verses beginning with "The two facing ones have sat down," using two verses for each direction and one in the middle.
In a water-vessel, he sprinkles around a stone, rice, and barley with two verses beginning "Be pleasant, O Earth," and with two verses beginning "O you who are well-strung."

With a branch of the *śamī* tree and one of the *palāśa*, he wipes it upward three times with the two verses beginning "Be pleasant, O Earth," with the two verses beginning "May we be well-protected," and with the three verses beginning "Homage be to the serpents."
This is that which is auspicious on all sides; this is vigor, this is essence.
Having thus attained human desires, you shall obtain that which is beyond the reach of the head.
Having thus poured [the water] on the middle pillar, he pours it into the pit.
Stay right here, O Tilvalā, most firmly established in stability! In the midst of nourishment, may the overflowing jar bring you to full bloom.
I have brought the vessel of curds together with the offspring of the world, O Vatsa.
Thus he addresses the middle pillar.
With the formula, "Thee for the Vasus, for the power of the Vasus, for day and night," he places a pillar into the pit.
Without a pillar, O Agni, ascend the beam; establish the Virāj and the Śakra.

The remaining pillars and beams are left silent.
Having measured out a house with either an eastern door or a southern door, he enters it with the verse, "I enter the houses with a cheerful mind; indeed, [a hero]," as explained previously.
King Varuṇa has come forth with the wealthy ones; let him stand in this place, prospering. Carrying nourishment and sprinkling ghee, may we dwell together among them with a well-disposed mind.
Thus, in the northeastern direction, he places a water-pot for the washing of the feet.
"I send you forth to the ocean; go back to your own source. May our heroes remain unharmed; let not my milk be spilled.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (morsel-offering) of rice in milk for Vāstoṣpati, he offers it with these two verses: "O Vāstoṣpati, the dispeller of disease... and "O Vāstoṣpati, grant us protection..."; and [the verse]:
"O Vāstoṣpati, furthering us, increasing our household with cattle and horses, O Indu..."
May you be free from old age in our friendship; like a father toward his sons, be gracious toward us.

O Vāstoṣpati, may we ever abide with you in auspicious, joyous, and path-providing fellowship; protect us in rest and in exertion, grant us our desire, and do you all protect us always with blessings.

Twelfth Section: One should offer the *bali* at evening and morning from the prepared food of the *vaiśvadeva*.
The oblation is prescribed as follows: to Agni and Soma, to Dhanvantari, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Then he offers the Bali-oblation: "Homage to Agni, to Soma, to Dhanvantari, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"—thus in the fire-chamber, each subsequent offering to the north of the preceding.
With the words "To the waters," he offers near the water-jar.
"To the herbs" [he offers] at the central pillar of the house; "to the trees" [he offers] at the central pillar of the house. (ManGS 2.12.5)
"To the deities of the household," [he says] in the middle of the house.
"To Dharma" and "to Adharma" at the door.
"To Death for the ether!"—thus [he offers] in the ether.
"To him who is within the cow-pen" means in the cow-pen. (ManGS 2.12.9)
"To Vaiśravaṇa, the possessor of the sacrificial grass"—with these words, he places [the grass] outside, facing eastward.
"To all the gods," [he says] at the dwelling.

"To Yama and to the messengers of Yama," [he says] to the south.

"To Soma, to the Soma-men," [he says] to the north.
"To Brahman, to the attendants of Brahman," [he says] in the middle.

"To the eastern [beings], to the Āpātikas, to the Sampātikas, to the Ṛkṣas, to the Yakṣas, to the Pipīlikās, to the Piśācas, to the Apsarases, to the Gandharvas, to the Guhyakas, to the Śailas, to the Pannagas, to the beings who roam by day—to the beings who roam by day and night," he says during the day; "to the beings who roam at night," he says at night. (ManGS 2.12.18)
To Dhanvantari, the libation for Dhanvantari.
Having mixed the remainder with water, he should pour it on the ground toward the south, saying, "Svadhā to the ancestors."
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should feed the guest and then eat what remains.

Thirteenth Section.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the sixth day.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, facing westward, he should eat food fit for an oblation.
The student, observing celibacy, should sleep on darbha grass or on rice husks with his head toward the east.
When the next day has dawned and the sun has risen, he should not refuse bathing, drinking, eating, ointments, garlands, or garments.

One should eat as much as is given, and one should eat whatever is given; however, one must avoid impure things, those who have committed mortal sins, and food offered by those who are obsessed with worldly desires.

When the sun has set, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* in milk, he then offers oblations with these names: "O Śakra, be pleased with me— [with] the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the giver of wealth, the mistress of the Vasus, the granter of desires for all who long for them, the meritorious and glorious one."
May Nandī, Bhūti, Lakṣmī, Ādityā, Yaśasvinī, Sumanā, Vāk, and Siddhi— the sixth— grant me wealth.
May the consumer of oblations grant me sons, cattle, wealth, grain, and many horses, goats, and sheep, as well as whatever has been mentally intended by me.
May the night that bestows wealth, the omniform Ṣaṣṭhī, come to me with riches; may Ṣaṣṭhī, who fulfills desires and is the consort of Kāma, grant me wealth.
Ākṛti, Prakṛtivarcasī, Dhāvanī, Padmacāriṇī—be intent on me, svāhā!
I invoke here Śrī, who has the fragrance as her door, who is invincible, ever-nourishing, rich in sacrificial offerings, and the sovereign of all beings—
she who possesses various leaves.
May that goddess Puṣṭi, who is exceedingly Sarasvatī, resort to the goddess Ari; may she bring wealth to me.
O Goddess, from the golden enclosure, may the boon come to me—long life and glory; svāhā!
I invoke the goddess Śrī, who is filled with horses, whose center is chariots, and who rejoices in the trumpeting of elephants; may the goddess Śrī be pleased with me.
May the hosts of gods and the serpents come to me along with ascetic power;
I have appeared in this kingdom— may Śrī bestow upon me faith (or fame, according to the Gaṅgādhara recension) and prosperity.
Svāhā to Śrī; svāhā to Hrī; svāhā to Lakṣmī.
Svāhā to Upalakṣmī, svāhā to Nanhā,
svāhā to Haridrā.
Hail to the sixth!
Hail to prosperity! Hail to victory!
"To Kāmā, svāhā! (ManGS 2.13.6)

He crushes a clod of earth.

he sees camels, pigs, donkeys, the *divākīrti* (the dog), and other such impure things in his dreams.
He strides across the intermediate space.
While walking on a road, he thinks, "Someone is following behind me."
Indeed, princes endowed with auspicious marks who are possessed by these Vināyakas do not obtain the kingdom.

Deer-earth, earth from a wild animal's den, earth from a bird's nest, yellow pigment, and bdellium.

Having prepared these ritual materials and mounted upon the bull-hide, he then [performs] this [consecration]:
"With those [waters] purified by the seers—the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed, purifying [waters]—I consecrate you; may the purifying verses (pāvamānī) cleanse you."
Given by Agni,
given by Indra,
given by Soma.
Given by Varuṇa, given by Vāyu,
given by Viṣṇu, given by Bṛhaspati.

Whatever misfortune is in your hair, in your parting, or on your head;

Fortune has been granted to you by King Varuṇa, by Bharga, by Sūrya, and by Bṛhaspati; fortune has also been bestowed by Indra, Vāyu, and the Seven Sages.

At night, having consecrated mustard oil that has been immediately pressed, he offers four oblations with a ladle made of udumbara wood:
(Oṃ) svāhā to Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, svāhā to Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputra, svāhā to Usmita.
"To the place of sacrifice, svāhā! (ManGS 2.14.27)
Thereafter, at a crossroads of villages, a crossroads of towns, or a crossroads of market-towns, having spread out *darbha* grass facing in all directions,

he offers an oblation in a new winnowing basket consisting of: husked rice, unhusked rice, raw meat, cooked meat, raw fish, cooked fish, raw cakes, cooked cakes, ground fragrances, and unground fragrances.

The drinking of honey, the drinking of *maireya*, the drinking of *surā*; loose garlands, woven garlands, red garlands, white garlands; garments that are red, yellow, white, black, blue, green, or variegated; and those that are speckled, with fringes at the base and borders. (ManGS 2.14.28)

Now, the invocation of the gods: Vimukha, Śyena, Baka, Yakṣa, Kalaha, Bhīru, Vināyaka, Kūṣmāṇḍarāj, Yajñāvikṣepī, Kulaṅgāpamāra, Yūpakeśī, Sūparakroḍī, Haimavata, Jambhaka, Virūpākṣa, Lohitākṣa, Vaiśravaṇa, Mahāsena, Mahādeva, and Mahārāja—may these gods of mine be pleased; being pleased, may they please me; being satisfied, may they satisfy me. O Varṇavatī, grant me complexion."
O Rūpavatī, grant me beauty;
O Tejasvinī, grant me splendor;
O Yaśasvinī, grant me fame.
"O thou who hast sons, grant me sons;

Fifteenth Section:

And Asvapna and Mānavadrāṇa shall protect [us] from the south.
May Gopāyana and Rakṣamāṇa protect me from behind;
may Jāgṛvi and Arundhatī protect me from the north.
May Viṣṇu, the Earth, and the Nāgas protect me from below;
may Bṛhaspati, the Viśvedevas, and the Sky protect me from above. (ManGS 2.15.1)
Thus, when such [an event] has occurred, one should suspect misfortunes.
Having offered sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should undertake a period of austerity for twelve nights, six nights, three nights, or one night.
If one should consider it an omen, then that [same rite] [should be performed].

If the sacrificial ladle should burn, or be destroyed, or fall down, or break, or laugh, or move;
or if one vessel should pour its contents into another, or the southern or northern vessel should break, or the northern vessel should be fixed upon a stone, or a door-beam should split;
or if a cow should suckle another cow—[in these cases, the rite must be performed again].
Or a woman may strike another woman [with] a knife-blade or with a ploughshare.
In the event of a thunderbolt falling, or if a pestle should shatter, or upon any other such marvel, one should offer oblations with these [verses]:
"May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being."
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
May the Aśvins and Bhaga measure out well-being for us; may the goddess Aditi, who is free from enemies, grant us well-being.
May Pūṣan, the Asura, grant us well-being; may Heaven and Earth, with their gracious intent, grant us well-being.
For our well-being, we invoke Vāyu; for our well-being, Soma, who is the lord of the world;
Bṛhaspati with his entire host for our well-being; may the Ādityas be for our well-being.
May all the gods today grant us well-being; may Agni Vaiśvānara, the Vasu, grant us well-being.
May the divine Ṛbhus protect us for our well-being; may Rudra preserve us from evil for our well-being.
May there be well-being for us in the forests and on the desert wastes; may there be well-being in the waters and in the dwelling place of the sun;
may there be well-being for us in the paths and in the wombs prepared for us; may he grant us well-being for wealth through the mind.
Indra the protector;
may this not be thine;
O Indra, let it perish.
"Like a formidable deer," "We choose that which is for our welfare"— with these [mantras], there are ten oblations.
From the word "victory" onwards, it is the same.

Sixteenth Section:

Fearing snakes, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having silently baked a cake on one potsherd for Bhauma and having ground unbroken barley-meal, he spreads darbha grass upon a naturally formed mound and offers it with the formula: "Svāhā to Acyuta, to Dhruva, to Bhauma! (ManGS 2.16.1).
He worships with the formulas "Homage to thee" and so forth, using two verses for each direction and one in the middle.
He offers an oblation of serpents with unhusked barley flour, saying: "To Īśāna," according to some;
"Thou art a serpent, the overlord of serpents; in thee are all serpents.
Let this offering of food be for the serpents; homage be to them! May they not harm me, may they not injure me, may they not kill me; I am not a serpent."

O Agni, do not release your wrath upon the one who offers oblations, nor upon the hostile enemy, nor upon misfortune; O powerful one, do not deliver us over to the one who strikes with his teeth, nor to the one who bites, nor to the one who seeks to harm us.
You are a serpent, the lord of serpents; with your jewel you protect human beings, and with your cake you protect the serpents.
May the serpents not harm that which is in you, nor that which is in me; may they not injure us, may they not kill us, and may they not bite us.
And with the three verses beginning "Homage be to the serpents" (namo astu sarpebhyaḥ).
"Stable I entrust this one to you," [he says], naming all his ministers and himself.
Having offered the snake-oblation according to this rite for four months, he desists.
Even when silent, the low-born woman should wash her hands.

Seventeenth Section:

If a dove, distressed by fear and not belonging to a flock, enters the house and its footprint is seen in the fire, one should offer oblations of curd, parched grain, or clarified butter while reciting the verse "devāḥ kapota" for each line, or one should sacrifice with it; [the verse begins] "devāḥ kapota iṣito yadicchan dūto."
This has come from Nirṛti; let us therefore offer praise to it and perform atonement. May there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
May the dove sent by Śiva be auspicious to us; O gods, may this bird be harmless in our homes.
May Agni, the wise one, accept our oblation, and may the flight of the bird avoid us.
The winged missile does not deceive us; it makes its place in the ash-heap, in the fire-chamber.
O gods, may the dove bring us well-being for our cattle and our men; let it not harm us here.
That which the owl speaks is in vain, as is that which the pigeon makes its footprint in the fire;
to him whose messenger this has been sent—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage.
Drive away the dove with a *ṛc*-verse; rejoicing in the sacrificial food, lead it around the cow.
Destroying all misfortunes, let it fly away from us, leaving behind its strength, as it settles down.
Thus [ends] ManGS 2.17.1.
Taking up the footprint, they carry it toward the south-west.
They go together with their legal disputes.
Having placed his foot step by step upon the saline soil he has prepared himself.
With the three verses beginning "From every abode," they drive out the impurities beyond the cow-pen.
They return without looking back.
Having returned, they mutter: "O Agni, you purify lives," "Agni is the seer," and "O Agni, purify yourself. (ManGS 2.17.7)
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the second [chapter].
The eighteenth [chapter]: On the first lunar day, one desiring a son should offer six oblations to Śaṇḍa.
Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* offering in milk, he makes an oblation of it with [the verse]: "May Agni, in agreement with the *brahman*, the slayer of *rakṣases*, drive away the affliction from here—
those ill-named ones who have settled upon your womb or your embryo."
Whoever, whether of evil name or otherwise, has settled upon the embryo or the womb—
Agni, together with the sacred word (brahman), having emerged, has destroyed him.
He who seeks to kill you as you fly, or as you sit, or as you crawl; he who seeks to destroy you once you are born—him we cause to perish from here.
Whoever lies down after having deluded you with sleep and darkness,
and whoever seeks to destroy your offspring— him we cause to perish from here.
Those Gandharvas who strike at the waters and those who dwell in the cow-pens—
we cause that flesh-eating, god-defying sorcerer to perish from here.
He who spreads his thighs apart, he who lies between the husband and wife,
and he who licks the vulva— him we cause to perish from here.
May her eggs be unbroken, may her fetus reach full growth, may she be free from misfortune, and may this female sow give birth and bring forth offspring; may she become prolific.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;
may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Conceive a fetus, O Sītā; conceive a fetus, O Vālinī!
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow a fetus upon you.
O Aśvins, you churned him forth from the golden fire-drills;
we invoke that embryo of yours for birth in the tenth month.
Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is distinct from the path of the gods;
I speak to you who have eyes and hear: do not harm our offspring nor our heroes.
Thus, six of these [twelve] are for the *sthālīpāka*—beginning with the first—and six are for the clarified butter (*ājya*). ManGS_2,18.2 //
From the word "jaya" onwards, it is the same [as in the preceding ritual].
Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* sacrifice for *naijam-eṣa*, he offers it according to the six-fold oblation:
"O *naijam-eṣa*, fly away; as one with good sons, fly back again!
Bestow upon this woman who desires a son that male child."
Just as this earth, lying supine, has received my embryo,
so do you receive that embryo to bring it forth in the tenth month.
O Viṣṇu, with your most excellent form, place a male child within this woman’s womb, so that he may be born in the tenth month.
Having performed the *pākayajñas*, which have a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*), a single layer of sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
and a single *sviṣṭakṛt* offering— even when there are various deities, even when there are various deities— ManGS 2.18.4.
